# Q1_0 layout evolution: upstream vs standard RVV vs Andes vd4dot

This note is visualisation-ready source material. It describes the three Q1_0
layouts relevant to the RISC-V CPU path and why they differ.

Scope: Q1_0 weights and Q8_0 activations, from the upstream non-repacked dot
kernel through the 64-output-row standard-RVV and Andes vd4dot repacked kernels.

## Executive summary

There are three states, not two. The first is the upstream source layout. The
latter two preserve the same mathematical Q1_0 values and occupy exactly the
same 1152 bytes per 64-row x 128-column weight tile, but permute 1024 sign
bits differently:

| property | Upstream Q1_0 | Standard RVV repack | Andes XAndesVDot repack (`Q1_VD4DOT`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| storage unit | one 128-K block for one output row | one 128-K block for 64 output rows | one 128-K block for 64 output rows |
| sign-bit grouping | sequential K signs inside one row | one K column x 64 rows | four adjacent K columns x 64 rows |
| sign-bit access/index | `row block + c / 8`, bit `c % 8` | `c * 64 + j` | `(c / 4) * 256 + 4 * j + (c % 4)` |
| VLEN=1024 useful parallel work | 32 i8 K lanes of one row | 64 output-row lanes | 64 rows x 4 i8 values, consumed as 64 vd4dot lanes |
| reduction | horizontal 32-lane reduction, four times per 128 K block | no horizontal reduction | no horizontal reduction inside the vd4dot instruction |
| natural vector view | 32-K signs of one row | 64-bit RVV mask for one K column | 256-byte i8 vector: 64 lanes x 4 K columns |
| integer work | select `+a[c]` or `-a[c]`, then reduce | select `+a[c]` or `-a[c]`, then add vertically | `nds.vd4dots.vv`: 4 signed i8 products into each i32 lane |
| minimum specialised VLEN | 128 bits | 512 bits | 1024 bits |
| compatible buffer | source model layout | Standard RVV only | Q1_VD4DOT only; must repack |

The important distinction is this:

```text
upstream layout optimises compact per-row storage
standard RVV repack optimises cross-row mask loading
Andes vd4dot repack optimises the 4-byte dot-product operand shape
```

## Shared Q1_0 data model

The original Q1_0 block represents 128 weights:

```text
block_q1_0, 18 bytes
+----------------+------------------------------------------------+
| d: fp16, 2 B    | qs: 128 sign bits = 16 B                      |
+----------------+------------------------------------------------+

weight[c] = qs_bit[c] ? +d : -d
```

One Q1_0 block aligns with four Q8_0 activation blocks because Q8_0 has 32
int8 codes and one fp16 scale per block:

```text
Q1_0 weights:       128 K columns, one scale dx
Q8_0 activations:   [0..31] [32..63] [64..95] [96..127]
                     dy0     dy1      dy2       dy3
```

The repack gathers 64 original weight rows for one 128-column block into one
`block_q1_0x64`:

```text
block_q1_0x64, 1152 bytes = 64 x 18 bytes
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| d[0..63]: 64 fp16 scales = 128 B                                |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| qs: 64 rows x 128 sign bits = 8192 bits = 1024 B                |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

Output lane j corresponds to original weight row j.
```

The scales are stored identically in both variants: `d[j]` is the Q1_0 scale
for output row `j`. Only `qs` changes order.

## Upstream layout: one row at a time

The model file and ordinary CPU tensor use consecutive `block_q1_0` records.
For a 64-row x 128-K tile, memory is row-major at block granularity:

```text
row 0:  [ d0 | 128 sign bits for K0..K127 ]
row 1:  [ d1 | 128 sign bits for K0..K127 ]
...
row 63: [d63 | 128 sign bits for K0..K127 ]
```

This is compact and is ideal for independently reading a single matrix row,
but it does not put the signs for the same K column of many output rows next to
one another. The upstream RVV dot kernel therefore processes one output row at
a time. It splits the 128-K Q1_0 block into four 32-K Q8_0 groups:

```text
for each output row:
  for each 32-K Q8_0 group:
    load 32 sign bits as an RVV mask
    select +activation or -activation in 32 lanes
    horizontally reduce 32 lanes to one integer
    apply this group's Q8_0 scale
  apply the Q1_0 scale
```

### The VLEN=1024 limitation of upstream

The upstream RVV implementation deliberately requests exactly 32 i8 lanes for
one Q8_0 group. Its VLEN >= 256 branch stays at 32 lanes even when the machine
has VLEN=1024. A VLEN=1024 register can hold 128 i8 elements, so 96 lanes are
idle during select/negate work:

```text
VLEN=1024, i8 capacity: 128 lanes

upstream uses: [ active 0..31 ] [ idle 32..127                          ]
                |---- 32 ----| |--------------- 96 --------------------|

then:            [ 32 partial values ] -> horizontal reduction -> [ 1 sum ]
```

Thus two independent costs combine: 75 percent of potential i8 lanes are idle
at VLEN=1024, and the kernel performs a horizontal reduction plus scalar-scale
work four times for every 128-K Q1_0 block. The standard 64-row repack changes
the work axis from "32 K values of one row" to "one K value across 64 rows".
It fills useful lanes with output rows and turns the K reduction into vertical
accumulation over the loop.

## Standard RVV repack: column-major sign masks

The standard layout stores each K column's 64 output-row signs as a contiguous
64-bit mask:

```text
qs[c][0..7] = signs for K column c, rows 0..63

byte 0: rows  0.. 7       byte 4: rows 32..39
byte 1: rows  8..15       byte 5: rows 40..47
byte 2: rows 16..23       byte 6: rows 48..55
byte 3: rows 24..31       byte 7: rows 56..63
```

For sign bit of K column `c` and output row `j`:

```text
bit_index = c * 64 + j
```

Visual form for four columns:

```text
memory order:
  column 0: [row 0 ... row 63]  -> one 64-bit mask
  column 1: [row 0 ... row 63]  -> one 64-bit mask
  column 2: [row 0 ... row 63]  -> one 64-bit mask
  column 3: [row 0 ... row 63]  -> one 64-bit mask
```

For every activation code `a[c]`, the kernel does the same operation in all
64 row lanes:

```text
sign mask for column c
        |
        v
lane j: sign[j,c] ? +a[c] : -a[c]
        |
        v
int accumulator for output row j
```

This makes the Q1_0 bitstream directly usable by an RVV mask load (`vlm`). It
then uses a masked add/subtract sequence. There is no horizontal reduction:
the K reduction is accumulated vertically over time in each output-row lane.

At VLEN=512, the standard kernel uses 64 lanes through i16,m2 and f32,m4. At
VLEN >= 1024, it uses i16,m1 and f32,m2. Both shapes retain 64 output rows.

## Andes Q1_VD4DOT repack: 4 K columns packed into each row lane

`nds.vd4dots.vv` consumes four i8 products per destination i32 lane:

```text
acc[j] += w[4*j + 0] * a[4*j + 0]
        + w[4*j + 1] * a[4*j + 1]
        + w[4*j + 2] * a[4*j + 2]
        + w[4*j + 3] * a[4*j + 3]
```

Therefore Q1_VD4DOT groups four adjacent K columns before arranging signs by rows.
For group `p = c / 4`, the 32 bytes are:

```text
byte address in group p:    4*j + r
contains sign for:          output row j, K column (4*p + r)

row 0:  [sign(0,4p+0), sign(0,4p+1), sign(0,4p+2), sign(0,4p+3)]
row 1:  [sign(1,4p+0), sign(1,4p+1), sign(1,4p+2), sign(1,4p+3)]
...
row 63: [sign(63,4p+0),sign(63,4p+1),sign(63,4p+2),sign(63,4p+3)]
```

Equivalently, the bit index is:

```text
bit_index = (c / 4) * 256 + 4 * j + (c % 4)
```

The signs first expand to i8 values `-1` or `+1`. With activation quadruple
`[a[4p], a[4p+1], a[4p+2], a[4p+3]]` broadcast into every row lane, the dot
instruction produces this exact value:

```text
acc[j] += sign[j,4p+0] * a[4p+0]
        + sign[j,4p+1] * a[4p+1]
        + sign[j,4p+2] * a[4p+2]
        + sign[j,4p+3] * a[4p+3]
```

The four signs are thus not a mask for four separate vector operations. They
are four neighbouring bytes in one dot-product lane.

The specialised Q1_VD4DOT implementation requires VLEN >= 1024. At e32,m2 that
is exactly 64 i32 lanes (the 64 output rows); viewed as e8,m2, the same group
contains 256 i8 elements (64 rows x 4 columns).

## Layout comparison on a 4-column x 4-row example

Let `S(j,c)` denote the sign bit of output row `j`, K column `c`.

```text
Logical matrix, same in both cases

              K0       K1       K2       K3
row 0       S(0,0)   S(0,1)   S(0,2)   S(0,3)
row 1       S(1,0)   S(1,1)   S(1,2)   S(1,3)
row 2       S(2,0)   S(2,1)   S(2,2)   S(2,3)
row 3       S(3,0)   S(3,1)   S(3,2)   S(3,3)

Upstream physical order: complete row blocks
  row 0: S(0,0) S(0,1) S(0,2) S(0,3)
  row 1: S(1,0) S(1,1) S(1,2) S(1,3)
  row 2: S(2,0) S(2,1) S(2,2) S(2,3)
  row 3: S(3,0) S(3,1) S(3,2) S(3,3)
  -> efficient for one independent output-row dot

Standard RVV physical order: columns first
  S(0,0) S(1,0) S(2,0) S(3,0) | S(0,1) S(1,1) S(2,1) S(3,1)
  S(0,2) S(1,2) S(2,2) S(3,2) | S(0,3) S(1,3) S(2,3) S(3,3)
  -> each column is one mask over rows

Andes Q1_VD4DOT physical order: rows first within a 4-column group
  S(0,0) S(0,1) S(0,2) S(0,3) | S(1,0) S(1,1) S(1,2) S(1,3)
  S(2,0) S(2,1) S(2,2) S(2,3) | S(3,0) S(3,1) S(3,2) S(3,3)
  -> each row is one 4-byte dot-product lane
```

## Execution and activation-side differences

Shared structure:

```text
for each 128-K weight block:
  load dx[64]
  for each of four Q8_0 groups of 32 K values:
    produce 64 integer partial sums
    multiply by group activation scale dy
  multiply by per-row weight scale dx
```

The differences are specifically in how a 32-element Q8_0 group is consumed:

| part | Standard RVV | Andes Q1_VD4DOT |
|---|---|---|
| K inner unit | one K column | four adjacent K columns |
| sign use | 64-lane mask selects `+a` or `-a` | mask expands signs to i8 `+1/-1` weights |
| arithmetic | 32 masked add/subtract steps per Q8 group | 8 four-way dot steps per Q8 group |
| activation broadcast | scalar i16 value into add/subtract | one packed 32-bit activation quad splatted with `vmv.v.x` |
| GEMM M tile | normal RVV handles 2 or 4 output activation rows by VLEN | vd4dot handles 4 rows together, sharing each weight vector |

For GEMV, `block_q8_0::qs` starts at byte offset 2. A 32-bit activation-quad
load would be misaligned for alternating blocks on the target core. The vd4dot

activation rows, because each dot operand needs consecutive K values for one
activation row. This is activation-side preparation, not a different Q1_0
weight layout.

  128 and whose output-row dimension is divisible by 64.

- Source model weights stay in the ordinary upstream Q1_0 format. The standard
  or vd4dot permutation is applied only while creating the CPU backend's repacked
  buffer.

# Q1_0 layout evolution: upstream vs standard RVV vs Andes vd4dot

This note is visualisation-ready source material. It describes the three Q1_0
layouts relevant to the RISC-V CPU path and why they differ.

Scope: Q1_0 weights and Q8_0 activations, from the upstream non-repacked dot
kernel through the 64-output-row standard-RVV and Andes vd4dot repacked kernels.

## Executive summary

There are three states, not two. The first is the upstream source layout. The
latter two preserve the same mathematical Q1_0 values and occupy exactly the
same 1152 bytes per 64-row x 128-column weight tile, but permute 1024 sign
bits differently:

| property | Upstream Q1_0 | Standard RVV repack | Andes XAndesVDot repack (`Q1_VD4DOT`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| storage unit | one 128-K block for one output row | one 128-K block for 64 output rows | one 128-K block for 64 output rows |
| sign-bit grouping | sequential K signs inside one row | one K column x 64 rows | four adjacent K columns x 64 rows |
| sign-bit access/index | `row block + c / 8`, bit `c % 8` | `c * 64 + j` | `(c / 4) * 256 + 4 * j + (c % 4)` |
| VLEN=1024 useful parallel work | 32 i8 K lanes of one row | 64 output-row lanes | 64 rows x 4 i8 values, consumed as 64 vd4dot lanes |
| reduction | horizontal 32-lane reduction, four times per 128 K block | no horizontal reduction | no horizontal reduction inside the vd4dot instruction |
| natural vector view | 32-K signs of one row | 64-bit RVV mask for one K column | 256-byte i8 vector: 64 lanes x 4 K columns |
| integer work | select `+a[c]` or `-a[c]`, then reduce | select `+a[c]` or `-a[c]`, then add vertically | `nds.vd4dots.vv`: 4 signed i8 products into each i32 lane |
| minimum specialised VLEN | 128 bits | 512 bits | 1024 bits |
| compatible buffer | source model layout | Standard RVV only | Q1_VD4DOT only; must repack |

The important distinction is this:

```text
upstream layout optimises compact per-row storage
standard RVV repack optimises cross-row mask loading
Andes vd4dot repack optimises the 4-byte dot-product operand shape
```

## Shared Q1_0 data model

The original Q1_0 block represents 128 weights:

```text
block_q1_0, 18 bytes
+----------------+------------------------------------------------+
| d: fp16, 2 B    | qs: 128 sign bits = 16 B                      |
+----------------+------------------------------------------------+

weight[c] = qs_bit[c] ? +d : -d
```

One Q1_0 block aligns with four Q8_0 activation blocks because Q8_0 has 32
int8 codes and one fp16 scale per block:

```text
Q1_0 weights:       128 K columns, one scale dx
Q8_0 activations:   [0..31] [32..63] [64..95] [96..127]
                     dy0     dy1      dy2       dy3
```

The repack gathers 64 original weight rows for one 128-column block into one
`block_q1_0x64`:

```text
block_q1_0x64, 1152 bytes = 64 x 18 bytes
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| d[0..63]: 64 fp16 scales = 128 B                                |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| qs: 64 rows x 128 sign bits = 8192 bits = 1024 B                |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

Output lane j corresponds to original weight row j.
```

The scales are stored identically in both variants: `d[j]` is the Q1_0 scale
for output row `j`. Only `qs` changes order.

## Upstream layout: one row at a time

The model file and ordinary CPU tensor use consecutive `block_q1_0` records.
For a 64-row x 128-K tile, memory is row-major at block granularity:

```text
row 0:  [ d0 | 128 sign bits for K0..K127 ]
row 1:  [ d1 | 128 sign bits for K0..K127 ]
...
row 63: [d63 | 128 sign bits for K0..K127 ]
```

This is compact and is ideal for independently reading a single matrix row,
but it does not put the signs for the same K column of many output rows next to
one another. The upstream RVV dot kernel therefore processes one output row at
a time. It splits the 128-K Q1_0 block into four 32-K Q8_0 groups:

```text
for each output row:
  for each 32-K Q8_0 group:
    load 32 sign bits as an RVV mask
    select +activation or -activation in 32 lanes
    horizontally reduce 32 lanes to one integer
    apply this group's Q8_0 scale
  apply the Q1_0 scale
```

### The VLEN=1024 limitation of upstream

The upstream RVV implementation deliberately requests exactly 32 i8 lanes for
one Q8_0 group. Its VLEN >= 256 branch stays at 32 lanes even when the machine
has VLEN=1024. A VLEN=1024 register can hold 128 i8 elements, so 96 lanes are
idle during select/negate work:

```text
VLEN=1024, i8 capacity: 128 lanes

upstream uses: [ active 0..31 ] [ idle 32..127                          ]
                |---- 32 ----| |--------------- 96 --------------------|

then:            [ 32 partial values ] -> horizontal reduction -> [ 1 sum ]
```

Thus two independent costs combine: 75 percent of potential i8 lanes are idle
at VLEN=1024, and the kernel performs a horizontal reduction plus scalar-scale
work four times for every 128-K Q1_0 block. The standard 64-row repack changes
the work axis from "32 K values of one row" to "one K value across 64 rows".
It fills useful lanes with output rows and turns the K reduction into vertical
accumulation over the loop.

## Standard RVV repack: column-major sign masks

The standard layout stores each K column's 64 output-row signs as a contiguous
64-bit mask:

```text
qs[c][0..7] = signs for K column c, rows 0..63

byte 0: rows  0.. 7       byte 4: rows 32..39
byte 1: rows  8..15       byte 5: rows 40..47
byte 2: rows 16..23       byte 6: rows 48..55
byte 3: rows 24..31       byte 7: rows 56..63
```

For sign bit of K column `c` and output row `j`:

```text
bit_index = c * 64 + j
```

Visual form for four columns:

```text
memory order:
  column 0: [row 0 ... row 63]  -> one 64-bit mask
  column 1: [row 0 ... row 63]  -> one 64-bit mask
  column 2: [row 0 ... row 63]  -> one 64-bit mask
  column 3: [row 0 ... row 63]  -> one 64-bit mask
```

For every activation code `a[c]`, the kernel does the same operation in all
64 row lanes:

```text
sign mask for column c
        |
        v
lane j: sign[j,c] ? +a[c] : -a[c]
        |
        v
int accumulator for output row j
```

This makes the Q1_0 bitstream directly usable by an RVV mask load (`vlm`). It
then uses a masked add/subtract sequence. There is no horizontal reduction:
the K reduction is accumulated vertically over time in each output-row lane.

At VLEN=512, the standard kernel uses 64 lanes through i16,m2 and f32,m4. At
VLEN >= 1024, it uses i16,m1 and f32,m2. Both shapes retain 64 output rows.

## Andes Q1_VD4DOT repack: 4 K columns packed into each row lane

`nds.vd4dots.vv` consumes four i8 products per destination i32 lane:

```text
acc[j] += w[4*j + 0] * a[4*j + 0]
        + w[4*j + 1] * a[4*j + 1]
        + w[4*j + 2] * a[4*j + 2]
        + w[4*j + 3] * a[4*j + 3]
```

Therefore Q1_VD4DOT groups four adjacent K columns before arranging signs by rows.
For group `p = c / 4`, the 32 bytes are:

```text
byte address in group p:    4*j + r
contains sign for:          output row j, K column (4*p + r)

row 0:  [sign(0,4p+0), sign(0,4p+1), sign(0,4p+2), sign(0,4p+3)]
row 1:  [sign(1,4p+0), sign(1,4p+1), sign(1,4p+2), sign(1,4p+3)]
...
row 63: [sign(63,4p+0),sign(63,4p+1),sign(63,4p+2),sign(63,4p+3)]
```

Equivalently, the bit index is:

```text
bit_index = (c / 4) * 256 + 4 * j + (c % 4)
```

The signs first expand to i8 values `-1` or `+1`. With activation quadruple
`[a[4p], a[4p+1], a[4p+2], a[4p+3]]` broadcast into every row lane, the dot
instruction produces this exact value:

```text
acc[j] += sign[j,4p+0] * a[4p+0]
        + sign[j,4p+1] * a[4p+1]
        + sign[j,4p+2] * a[4p+2]
        + sign[j,4p+3] * a[4p+3]
```

The four signs are thus not a mask for four separate vector operations. They
are four neighbouring bytes in one dot-product lane.

The specialised Q1_VD4DOT implementation requires VLEN >= 1024. At e32,m2 that
is exactly 64 i32 lanes (the 64 output rows); viewed as e8,m2, the same group
contains 256 i8 elements (64 rows x 4 columns).

## Layout comparison on a 4-column x 4-row example

Let `S(j,c)` denote the sign bit of output row `j`, K column `c`.

```text

row 0       S(0,0)   S(0,1)   S(0,2)   S(0,3)
row 1       S(1,0)   S(1,1)   S(1,2)   S(1,3)
row 2       S(2,0)   S(2,1)   S(2,2)   S(2,3)
row 3       S(3,0)   S(3,1)   S(3,2)   S(3,3)

Upstream physical order: complete row blocks
  row 0: S(0,0) S(0,1) S(0,2) S(0,3)
  row 1: S(1,0) S(1,1) S(1,2) S(1,3)
  row 2: S(2,0) S(2,1) S(2,2) S(2,3)
  row 3: S(3,0) S(3,1) S(3,2) S(3,3)
  -> efficient for one independent output-row dot

Standard RVV physical order: columns first
  S(0,0) S(1,0) S(2,0) S(3,0) | S(0,1) S(1,1) S(2,1) S(3,1)
  S(0,2) S(1,2) S(2,2) S(3,2) | S(0,3) S(1,3) S(2,3) S(3,3)
  -> each column is one mask over rows

Andes Q1_VD4DOT physical order: rows first within a 4-column group
  S(0,0) S(0,1) S(0,2) S(0,3) | S(1,0) S(1,1) S(1,2) S(1,3)
  S(2,0) S(2,1) S(2,2) S(2,3) | S(3,0) S(3,1) S(3,2) S(3,3)
  -> each row is one 4-byte dot-product lane
```

Shared structure:

```text
for each 128-K weight block:
  load dx[64]
  for each of four Q8_0 groups of 32 K values:
    produce 64 integer partial sums
    multiply by group activation scale dy
  multiply by per-row weight scale dx
```

The differences are specifically in how a 32-element Q8_0 group is consumed:

| part | Standard RVV | Andes Q1_VD4DOT |
|---|---|---|
| K inner unit | one K column | four adjacent K columns |
| sign use | 64-lane mask selects `+a` or `-a` | mask expands signs to i8 `+1/-1` weights |
| arithmetic | 32 masked add/subtract steps per Q8 group | 8 four-way dot steps per Q8 group |

| GEMM M tile | normal RVV handles 2 or 4 output activation rows by VLEN | vd4dot handles 4 rows together, sharing each weight vector |

activation rows, because each dot operand needs consecutive K values for one
activation row. This is activation-side preparation, not a different Q1_0
weight layout.

- Q1_VD4DOT has a specialised path only at VLEN >= 1024 and when built with

  repacked buffers are binary incompatible even though their size is equal.
- Source model weights stay in the ordinary upstream Q1_0 format. The standard
  or vd4dot permutation is applied only while creating the CPU backend's repacked
  buffer.

portable performance guarantee:

```text

standard RVV -> Andes vd4dots:         geometric mean 3.54x

| type traits (vec_dot_type) | `ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c:249` (q1_0), `:255` (q2_0), `:422`, `:428` (tq) |

## 1. Cheat sheet

| type | weights/block | block bytes | bits/weight | stored code | real value | activation side |
|--------|-----|--------------|--------|-------------------|---------------|-----------|
| Q1_0 | 128 | 2 + 16 = 18 | 1.125 | 1 bit `b` | `b ? +d : -d` | 4 x Q8_0 |
| Q2_0 | 64 | 2 + 16 = 18 | 2.25 | 2 bits `q` in 0..3 | `(q - 1) * d` | 2 x Q8_0 |
| TQ1_0 | 256 | 48 + 4 + 2 = 54 | 1.6875 | trit `t` in 0..2 | `(t - 1) * d` | 1 x Q8_K |
| TQ2_0 | 256 | 64 + 2 = 66 | 2.0625 | 2 bits `t` in 0..2 | `(t - 1) * d` | 1 x Q8_K |

One-line character of each:

- **Q1_0**: pure sign bits. Smallest, no zero value. The bit layout IS an RVV mask register image, so the kernel needs no unpack at all.
- **Q2_0**: plain 2-bit fields in element order. Simple scalar unpack, but the layout is not SIMD-friendly (see 3.3).
- **TQ1_0**: 5 trits per byte, base-3 arithmetic coding. Smallest ternary format; unpack costs one multiply chain per trit plane.
- **TQ2_0**: 2 bits per trit, plane-interleaved. 22% bigger than TQ1_0, but unpack is just shift + mask; the fastest ternary format on most SIMD.

Scales: `d` is fp16 in the weight block. Q1_0 uses `d = mean(|x|)` over the block; the other three use `d = max(|x|)`.

## 2. Shared ideas

A row of K weights is stored as K/QK blocks back to back (QK = 128, 64, 256, 256). Matmul never converts weights to float. The activation row is quantized once (`from_float` to the `vec_dot_type` above), then each `vec_dot` call does integer math inside a block and multiplies by the scales only at block edges:

```

content.content:
---
name: diagrams-need-a-worked-example
description: "Nick wants technical figures drawn to real scale so the problem is visible as area; not schematics, and not toy examples he has to hand-compute"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 8e533375-c955-49b0-8814-eb9d2ab88fa2
  modified: 2026-08-04T02:08:30.047Z
---

Two rejections on the same figure set, in order:

1. Schematic diagrams (random-looking cells, greyed grids showing only shape)
   got "so crude nobody can understand it".
2. My fix - an 8x8 worked example with checkable numbers - got rejected too:
   *"with these small examples you cannot see lane utilization. I want a
   diagram that is easy to understand, not one I have to hand-compute. You
   have to make people see where the problem is."*

**Why:** the figure has to carry the *problem*, and here the problem was
proportion - 32 of 128 lanes busy, 1 of 64 outputs advancing. Shrinking to a
toy size destroys exactly that. Numbers a reader must add up are work, not
explanation.

**How to apply:**

- Draw at the machine's real dimensions. 128 lanes means 128 lane slots; a
  64x128 tile means a 2:1 box. The empty space then *is* the waste.
- Encode the point as **area, count and colour**, never as arithmetic. A bar
  25% filled, a dot matrix with 1 of 64 lit, a shaded sliver in a big grid.
- Put the comparison in one figure, one row per variant, same axes - the
  reader sees the improvement without reading a single number.
- Values inside cells are usually noise. Show *how many* and *where*, not
  *what*.
- Still generate everything from a script owning the constants, with tests
  that the drawn geometry matches the printed labels. `example.py` /
  `test_example.py` in the Q1_0 page scratchpad is the working pattern.
- Render each SVG to PNG (rsvg-convert with the CSS vars substituted) and
  look at it. Overlapping labels are invisible in source.
- SVG `<pattern>` instead of thousands of rects when a bar has hundreds of
  cells; it kept the page at 218 KB instead of 285 KB.

Related: [[q1_0-wide-vlen-repack-rowparallel]],
[[xandesvdot-nds-vd4dots-usable]], [[keep-writeups-scoped-to-the-optimization]]
---
name: writeups-need-progressive-disclosure
description: "Nick reads technical pages top-down by level; each section must show a handful of blocks and hide the rest behind <details>, with support material at the end"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 8e533375-c955-49b0-8814-eb9d2ab88fa2
  modified: 2026-08-04T06:29:57.255Z
---

On the Q1_0 write-up (2026-08-04): *"the whole thing is still very messy. Go
step by step. Do not add too much information at once. Give information from
high level to low level - that is how it becomes clear."*

Two separate rules came out of that:

**1. Order the document by level, not by chronology.** The page had opened
with machine specs and measurement methodology - a reader met ten numbers
before learning what was slow. The fix:

- hero: one claim, one number, one picture of the problem
- then: the N changes and what each one bought, in one section
- then: the setup they operate on (the data format)
- then: one section per change
- then: measurements
- last: an appendix with the machine spec and how the numbers were taken

**2. Cap what a section shows at once.** Stage 04 was showing 19 blocks
(summary, prose, figure, five panels, two assembly listings, a tally, three
cards, three sub-headings). Now every section shows at most 7 and the rest
sits in `<details class="more">` with a descriptive summary. Visible = what
changed, the picture, the number. Hidden = assembly, byte layouts, instruction
tallies, side notes.

**Why:** he scans for the shape of the argument first and only then drills in.
A flat wall of equally-weighted blocks gives him no way to do that, no matter
how good the individual blocks are.

**How to apply:** guard it with a test that counts, per section, the blocks
outside `<details>` and fails above the cap - otherwise the page silently
re-densifies on the next edit. `test_page.py::visible_blocks` in the Q1_0
scratchpad is the working version. Also confirm each disclosure has a real
summary, not "More".

Related: [[diagrams-need-a-worked-example]],
[[keep-writeups-scoped-to-the-optimization]]
---
name: keep-writeups-scoped-to-the-optimization
description: "In Nick's perf write-ups, cut everything that is not the optimization itself - no traps, no \"did not work\", no corrections, no open items"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 8e533375-c955-49b0-8814-eb9d2ab88fa2
  modified: 2026-08-04T01:43:39.909Z
---

Nick's instruction on the Q1_0 write-up (2026-08-04): "remove information
unrelated to the optimization, like anything about fail - do not mention it."

What that removed from the page:

- A "Traps" section (silent DCE, stride-0 broadcast, misaligned load) and the
  build gates that catch them.
- "Did not work" cards describing approaches that were tried and reverted.
- A "Correction on the record" card retracting an earlier wrong claim.
- A "What is left" / open-items section.
- Every mention of a tensor that failed the repack gate, and the per-token
  roll-up was rescoped to only the layers that were actually optimized.

What stayed: the mechanism of each stage, the measured cycles, and the
constraints that shaped the kernel (stated as requirements, e.g. "this core
requires a 32-bit vector element load to be 4-byte aligned", not as "it
faults").

**Why:** the document's job is to explain how the speedup was obtained. War
stories about bugs, reverted experiments and unfinished work are a different
document and dilute this one.

**How to apply:** engineering-diary material belongs in ROADMAP.md or a memory,
not in the write-up. If a limitation must appear because a number depends on
it, state the scope positively and label it, rather than narrating the failure.

Related: [[diagrams-need-a-worked-example]]

content.content: Launching skill: artifact-design

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.content: Launching skill: artifact-diagramming

content.text:
Draw as the engineer who has to live with the decision, not as a decorator: a diagram earns its place when it lets a cold reader see a mechanism they would otherwise have to assemble from prose - where data flows, which components talk, what changes between two options, what state a request moves through. If a sentence says it faster, write the sentence.

## What to draw

**Depict the mechanism, not its name.** A box labeled "cache" says less than the prose; the path a request takes through it, the two stores it sits between, and the arrow that disappears when the cache is removed say what the words can't. Show the parts that the argument hinges on - the boundary being crossed, the hop being added, the data that moves - and leave out the parts that don't.

**Comparing options?** Draw the difference. Two architectures side by side, a before and an after, the one edge that each option adds or removes - the reader should be able to point at what they are choosing between. A separate labeled box per option, with nothing connecting them to the system, is not a comparison; it is a restated option list.

**Match complexity to the stakes.** A one-hop question is a three-box diagram; a migration that reroutes writes through a queue needs the queue, the writer, the reader, and the ordering arrow. Draw as much as the decision actually turns on - no forced minimalism, no inventory of the whole system either.

**Label the arrows.** An unlabeled arrow is "related somehow"; `writes`, `invalidates`, `polls every 30s` is information. A legend is only worth it when the same encoding (dashed, colored, doubled) repeats; otherwise put the meaning on the mark itself.

## Inline SVG mechanics

These mechanics apply where the page renders inline SVG natively (HTML pages); a markdown-rendered page draws its diagrams in whatever fence that lane's renderer supports, and the skill that owns the lane says which. Hand-author inline `<svg>` with native shapes (`rect`, `circle`, `line`, `polyline`, `path`) and `<text>` - no libraries, no runtime, no external images.

- **Size by `viewBox`.** Set `viewBox="0 0 W H"` and let CSS scale it (`max-width: 100%; height: auto`); choose W and H for the content, not a preset. Wide flows read left-to-right; layered stacks read top-to-bottom.
- **Theme with `currentColor`.** Strokes, text, and arrowheads in `currentColor` inherit the page's foreground in light and dark themes alike; reserve a literal hue for the one element that carries meaning (the option leaned toward, the hop under discussion), and make sure it reads on both grounds.
- **Arrowheads are markers or polygons.** A `<defs><marker>` referenced by `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` (fragment-internal id) or a small `<polygon>` at the line's end - never an image.
- **Keep text legible.** Roughly 11-13px at the drawn scale, `text-anchor` for alignment, short labels (a word or three); explanatory sentences belong in the caption below the figure, not in the drawing.
- **Align to a grid.** Shared baselines and even gaps are most of what makes a hand diagram read as deliberate; eyeballed offsets read as noise.
- **One figure, one claim.** Wrap the `<svg>` in `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states what the picture shows, and give the `<svg>` `role="img"` plus an `aria-label` carrying the same claim for readers who cannot see it.
- **Stay self-contained.** No `<script>`, `<style>`, or `<foreignObject>` inside the SVG; gradients, patterns, and `<use>` reference ids in the same fragment (`href="#id"`). Long decorative path data is a sign the drawing wants a real graphics tool - simplify instead.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate the "One Q1_0 Tile, Three Layouts" page.

Every drawn width on the page derives from the constants below, and every
source excerpt is cut from the repo at build time, so the page cannot drift
from the kernels it explains.
"""
from pathlib import Path
import html
import random

REPO = Path("/home/nick/work/llama.cpp")
OUT = Path(__file__).with_name("q1_0_layout_page.html")

# ---- format and machine constants ------------------------------------------
QK1, QK8, ROWS = 128, 32, 64
VLENB = 128                              # VLEN = 1024 bits
BLOCK_Q1 = 2 + QK1 // 8                  # 18 B: fp16 d + 128 sign bits
BLOCK_Q8 = 2 + QK8                       # 34 B: fp16 d + 32 int8
BLOCK_Q8X4 = 4 * 2 + 4 * QK8             # 136 B: 4 fp16 d + 4 x 32 int8 (interleaved)
BLOCK_Q1X64 = ROWS * BLOCK_Q1            # 1152 B
SCALE_BYTES = ROWS * 2                   # 128 B of fp16 scales at the block front
SIGN_BYTES = BLOCK_Q1X64 - SCALE_BYTES   # 1024 B = 64 x 128 bits


def sign_bit_rvv(c, j):
    """repack.h q1_0x64_sign_bit, default order: column-major planes."""
    return c * ROWS + j


def sign_bit_vd4(c, j):
    """repack.h q1_0x64_sign_bit, Q1_VD4DOT order: 4 columns per lane."""
    return (c // 4) * 256 + 4 * j + (c % 4)


VARIANTS = ["upstream", "rvv", "vd4"]
NAME = {"upstream": "Upstream", "rvv": "RVV repack", "vd4": "VD4DOT repack"}
COL = {"upstream": "var(--up)", "rvv": "var(--rvv)", "vd4": "var(--vd4)"}
COL_LT = {"upstream": "var(--up-lt)", "rvv": "var(--rvv-lt)", "vd4": "var(--vd4-lt)"}
SCALE, SCALE_LT = "var(--scale)", "var(--scale-lt)"
ACT, ACT_LT = "var(--act)", "var(--act-lt)"
ACT_ROW = ["var(--m0)", "var(--m1)", "var(--m2)", "var(--m3)"]
TRACK, LINE, INK, MUTED, PAPER = "var(--track)", "var(--line)", "currentColor", "var(--muted)", "var(--paper)"

# what ONE vlm.v pulls from the sign region
FOOTPRINT_BYTES = {"upstream": 4, "rvv": 8, "vd4": 32}
FOOTPRINT_CELLS = {"upstream": (32, 1), "rvv": (1, 64), "vd4": (4, 64)}   # (columns, rows)

# vector instructions per 64 rows x 32 K, read off the kernel inner loops
UNIT_OPS = {
    "upstream": (["vlm.v", "vle8.v", "vneg.v", "vmerge.vvm", "vwredsum.vs"], ROWS),   # per row
    "rvv":      (["vlm.v", "vsub.vx", "vadd.vx (masked)"], QK8),                      # per column
    "vd4":      (["vlm.v", "vmerge.vxm", "vmv.v.x", "nds.vd4dots.vv"], QK8 // 4),     # per 4-column quad
}
OPS_PER_SUBTILE = {v: len(ops) * n for v, (ops, n) in UNIT_OPS.items()}

# register bytes carrying useful lanes per instruction, VLEN = 1024
REG_AXIS = 2 * VLENB                                     # an m2 group, 256 B
REG_GROUP = {"upstream": VLENB, "rvv": VLENB, "vd4": 2 * VLENB}
REG_BUSY = {"upstream": 32, "rvv": 128, "vd4": 256}
REG_LABEL = {
    "upstream": "e8, m1: 32 of 128 lanes busy",
    "rvv": "e16, m1: 64 lanes, all busy",
    "vd4": "e8, m2: 256 lanes, all busy",
}
OUTCOME = {
    "upstream": "then vwredsum.vs: 32 lanes → 1 sum, for 1 row",
    "rvv": "64 row sums, each advances by 1 column",
    "vd4": "64 row sums, each advances by 4 columns",
}

# ---- drawing scales --------------------------------------------------------
W = 920
TILE_CELL = 2.25                      # hero: one sign bit
PX_REG = 288 / REG_AXIS               # hero: register byte
PX_OPS = 288 / max(OPS_PER_SUBTILE.values())
PX_STRIP = 0.75                       # weight memory strip byte
PX_FMT = 6                            # format strips byte
PX_FLOW = 8                           # flow figures: memory byte
PX_LANE8 = 2                          # flow figures: one i8 lane of an m2 group


def restaged_quad_offsets():
    """Byte offsets of the 32-bit activation quads in the aligned copy the vd4 gemv makes."""
    return [g * QK8 + 4 * q for g in range(4) for q in range(QK8 // 4)]


# ---- source excerpts -------------------------------------------------------
def excerpt(rel, start, end="}"):
    lines = (REPO / rel).read_text().splitlines()
    i = next(n for n, l in enumerate(lines) if start in l)
    j = next(n for n in range(i + 1, len(lines)) if lines[n] == end)
    return "\n".join(lines[i:j + 1])


def excerpt_range(rel, first, last):
    lines = (REPO / rel).read_text().splitlines()
    return "\n".join(lines[first - 1:last])


# ---- svg helpers -----------------------------------------------------------
def esc(s):
    return html.escape(str(s), quote=True)


def _attrs(a):
    return "".join(f' {k.replace("_", "-")}="{esc(v)}"' for k, v in a.items())


def R(x, y, w, h, fill, **a):
    return f'<rect x="{x:g}" y="{y:g}" width="{w:g}" height="{h:g}" fill="{fill}"{_attrs(a)}/>'


def T(x, y, s, size=12, anchor="start", fill=INK, weight="normal", **a):
    return (f'<text x="{x:g}" y="{y:g}" font-size="{size}" text-anchor="{anchor}" fill="{fill}" '
            f'font-weight="{weight}"{_attrs(a)}>{esc(s)}</text>')


def L(x1, y1, x2, y2, stroke=INK, width=1, dash=None, arrow=False):
    d = f' stroke-dasharray="{dash}"' if dash else ""
    m = ' marker-end="url(#arrow)"' if arrow else ""
    return f'<line x1="{x1:g}" y1="{y1:g}" x2="{x2:g}" y2="{y2:g}" stroke="{stroke}" stroke-width="{width}"{d}{m}/>'


def ARROW_DEF():
    return ('<marker id="arrow" viewBox="0 0 8 8" refX="7" refY="4" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">'
            '<path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker>')


def down(x, y1, y2, label=None, lx=None):
    s = L(x, y1, x, y2, arrow=True)
    if label:
        s += T((lx if lx is not None else x + 6), (y1 + y2) / 2 + 4, label, 11, fill=MUTED)
    return s


def svg(fid, w, h, body, label):
    return (f'<svg id="{fid}" viewBox="0 0 {w} {h}" role="img" aria-label="{esc(label)}">'
            f'<defs>{ARROW_DEF()}{body[0]}</defs>{body[1]}</svg>')


def sample_bits(n, seed):
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    return [rnd.random() < 0.5 for _ in range(n)]


def lanes(x, y, n, pitch, h, colors, gap=0.5):
    """n adjacent lane cells; colors is a list of fills, one per lane."""
    return "".join(R(x + i * pitch, y, max(pitch - gap, 0.5), h, colors[i]) for i in range(n))

def fig_hero():
    colw, gap = 288, 28
    tw, th = QK1 * TILE_CELL, ROWS * TILE_CELL
    y_title, y_tile = 14, 26
    y_foot = y_tile + th + 16
    y_reg = y_foot + 12
    y_regl = y_reg + 28
    y_out = y_regl + 20
    y_bar = y_out + 14
    y_barl = y_bar + 28
    H = y_barl + 8
    defs = (f'<pattern id="grid8" width="{8 * TILE_CELL:g}" height="{8 * TILE_CELL:g}" patternUnits="userSpaceOnUse">'
            f'<path d="M {8 * TILE_CELL:g} 0 L 0 0 0 {8 * TILE_CELL:g}" fill="none" stroke="{LINE}" stroke-width="0.6"/></pattern>')
    body = []
    for i, v in enumerate(VARIANTS):
        x0 = i * (colw + gap)
        body.append(R(x0, y_title - 10, 10, 10, COL[v]))
        body.append(T(x0 + 16, y_title, NAME[v], 13, weight="bold"))
        body.append(T(x0 + colw, y_title, "64 rows × 128 K", 11, anchor="end", fill=MUTED))
        body.append(R(x0, y_tile, tw, th, TRACK))
        body.append(R(x0, y_tile, tw, th, "url(#grid8)"))
        cols, rows = FOOTPRINT_CELLS[v]
        body.append(R(x0, y_tile, cols * TILE_CELL, rows * TILE_CELL, COL[v],
                      data_role="tilefoot", data_variant=v, data_cols=cols, data_rows=rows))
        body.append(T(x0, y_foot, f"one vlm.v = {cols * rows} sign bits: {rows} row{'s' if rows > 1 else ''} × {cols} column{'s' if cols > 1 else ''}",
                      11, data_for=f"tilefoot-{v}"))
        # register: 256-byte axis for all three
        body.append(R(x0, y_reg, REG_AXIS * PX_REG, 14, TRACK))
        body.append(R(x0, y_reg, REG_BUSY[v] * PX_REG, 14, COL[v], data_role="regbusy", data_variant=v, data_bytes=REG_BUSY[v]))
        body.append(R(x0, y_reg, REG_GROUP[v] * PX_REG, 14, "none", stroke=INK, stroke_width=1))
        body.append(T(x0, y_regl, REG_LABEL[v], 11, fill=MUTED))
        body.append(T(x0, y_out, OUTCOME[v], 11))
        n = OPS_PER_SUBTILE[v]
        body.append(R(x0, y_bar, n * PX_OPS, 14, COL[v], data_role="opsbar", data_variant=v, data_ops=n))
        body.append(T(x0, y_barl, f"{n} vector instructions per 64 rows × 32 K", 11, weight="bold", data_for=f"opsbar-{v}"))
    return svg("fig-hero", W, H, (defs, "".join(body)),
               "One vlm.v covers a 1x32 sliver upstream, a 64x1 column after the RVV repack and a 64x4 band after the "
               "VD4DOT repack; the register goes from 32 busy lanes to 256, and the instruction count per 64x32 sub-tile from 320 to 32.")

    body.append(T(p, y1 + 15, "d", 10, anchor="middle", fill="var(--on-mark)"))
    for k in range(4):
        x = 2 * p + k * 4 * p
        body.append(R(x, y1, 4 * p - 0.5, hh, COL["upstream"]))
        body.append(T(x + 2 * p, y1 + 15, f"k{k}", 10, anchor="middle", fill="var(--on-mark)"))
    body.append(T(BLOCK_Q1 * p + 8, y1 + 15, "qs[16]: byte b holds K = 8b .. 8b+7, LSB first (an RVV mask image)", 11, fill=MUTED))
    body.append(T(0, y2 - 9, "4 × block_q8_0 · 136 B · 128 activations: 4 fp16 scales + 128 int8 codes", 12, weight="bold"))
    body.append(R(0, y2, 4 * BLOCK_Q8 * p, hh, "none", data_role="fmt", data_variant="q8x4"))
    for k in range(4):
        x = k * BLOCK_Q8 * p
        body.append(R(x, y2, 2 * p, hh, SCALE))
        body.append(T(x + p, y2 + 15, "d", 10, anchor="middle", fill="var(--on-mark)"))
        body.append(R(x + 2 * p, y2, QK8 * p - 0.5, hh, ACT))
        body.append(T(x + 2 * p + QK8 * p / 2, y2 + 15, f"qs[32] of Q8 block k{k}: K = {32 * k} .. {32 * k + 31}", 10, anchor="middle", fill="var(--on-mark)"))
        # pairing lines: Q1 sub-segment k -> Q8 block k
        xa = 2 * p + k * 4 * p + 2 * p

    return svg("fig-formats", W, y2 + hh + 56, ("", "".join(body)),
               "A block_q1_0 is 18 bytes for 128 weights; the four block_q8_0 it pairs with are 136 bytes for 128 activations. "
               "Each 4-byte sub-segment of the Q1_0 sign bits pairs with one Q8_0 block.")

UPSTREAM_INNER = """// one output row y, one Q8_0 group k (32 K)                          register use at VLEN=1024
vbool8_t   m   = __riscv_vlm_v_b8(x[ib].qs + 4*k, 32);              // 4 B  -> 32 mask bits
vint8m1_t  qy  = __riscv_vle8_v_i8m1(yb->qs, 32);                   // 32 B -> lanes 0..31 of 128
vint8m1_t  nqy = __riscv_vneg_v_i8m1(qy, 32);                       // -a
vint8m1_t  sy  = __riscv_vmerge_vvm_i8m1(nqy, qy, m, 32);           // m ? +a : -a
vint16m1_t r   = __riscv_vwredsum_vs_i8m1_i16m1(sy, zero, 32);      // 32 lanes -> 1 (horizontal)
acc  += FP16_TO_FP32(yb->d) * (float) __riscv_vmv_x_s_i16m1_i16(r); // x d_a[k], scalar
// after the 4 groups of this 128-K block:
sumf += FP16_TO_FP32(x[ib].d) * acc;                                // x d_w, scalar"""

RVV_INNER = """// 64 output rows at once, one Q8_0 group k (32 K)
vint16m1_t sumi = __riscv_vmv_v_x_i16m1(0, 64);
for (int c = 0; c < 32; ++c) {
    const int16_t   yc   = ab->qs[c];                                        // 1 B scalar
    const vbool16_t sign = __riscv_vlm_v_b16(bx[l].qs[k*32 + c], 64);        // 8 B -> 64-lane mask
    sumi = __riscv_vsub_vx_i16m1(sumi, yc, 64);                              // every row:  -a[c]
    sumi = __riscv_vadd_vx_i16m1_mu(sign, sumi, sumi, (int16_t)(2*yc), 64);  // sign rows: +2a[c]
}
facc = __riscv_vfmacc_vf_f32m2(facc, FP16_TO_FP32(ab->d),                    // x d_a[k] on 64 lanes
           __riscv_vfcvt_f_x_v_f32m2(__riscv_vsext_vf2_i32m2(sumi, 64), 64), 64);
// after the 4 groups of this 128-K block:
sumf = __riscv_vfmacc_vv_f32m2(sumf, dx, facc, 64);                          // x d_w[0..63], one vector"""

VD4_INNER = """// 64 output rows at once, 4 quads = 16 K of group k
const uint8_t * p = planes + (k*8 + q) * 32;                                   // 4 planes x 32 B
vint8m2_t w0 = __riscv_vmerge_vxm_i8m2(vneg1, 1, __riscv_vlm_v_b4(p +  0, 256), 256); // 256 signs -> +-1 i8
vint8m2_t w1 = __riscv_vmerge_vxm_i8m2(vneg1, 1, __riscv_vlm_v_b4(p + 32, 256), 256);
vint8m2_t w2 = __riscv_vmerge_vxm_i8m2(vneg1, 1, __riscv_vlm_v_b4(p + 64, 256), 256);
vint8m2_t w3 = __riscv_vmerge_vxm_i8m2(vneg1, 1, __riscv_vlm_v_b4(p + 96, 256), 256);
acc = q1_vd4dots_x4_m2(acc, w0, w1, w2, w3, aw[q], aw[q+1], aw[q+2], aw[q+3]);  // aw: uint32 quads

// q1_vd4dots_x4_m2: GCC 14.2 has no intrinsic for the dot, so the e32 half is one asm block
vsetvli t0, zero, e32, m2, ta, ma      // one vtype covers the four dots and their broadcasts
vmv.v.x        s0, u0                  // 4-byte activation quad -> all 64 i32 lanes (from a GPR)
vmv.v.x        s1, u1
nds.vd4dots.vv acc, w0, s0             // acc[j] += sum_{r<4} w0[4j+r] * s0[4j+r]
nds.vd4dots.vv acc, w1, s1
vmv.v.x        s0, u2
vmv.v.x        s1, u3
nds.vd4dots.vv acc, w2, s0
nds.vd4dots.vv acc, w3, s1
// after 8 quads: facc = vfmacc_vf(facc, d_a[k], vfcvt_f_x(acc));  after 4 groups: sumf = vfmacc_vv(sumf, dx, facc)"""

<h1>One Q1_0 tile, three memory layouts</h1>
<p class="sub">The same 64-row × 128-K weight tile is stored three ways. <h2>What changes from one layout to the next</h2>
<p>Three things move together: the order of the sign bits in memory, the shape of the activation operand, and the instruction that joins them. The scales do not move; they are only read differently.</p>
<div class="tw"><table>
<tr><th></th><th><span class="chip up">Upstream</span></th><th><span class="chip rvv">RVV repack</span></th><th><span class="chip vd4">VD4DOT repack</span></th></tr>

<tr><td>one vlm.v reads</td><td>4 B: 32 K of 1 row</td><td>8 B: 1 K of 64 rows</td><td>32 B: 4 K of 64 rows</td></tr>
<tr><td>weight scale</td><td>fp16 inside each record, scalar</td><td>d[64] at block front, one vector</td><td>d[64] at block front, one vector</td></tr>
<tr><td>activation operand</td><td>32 int8 in a vector</td><td>1 int8 as a scalar (.vx)</td><td>4 int8 as one 32-bit GPR, splat</td></tr>
<tr><td>activation scale</td><td>fp16 per 32 K, scalar multiply</td><td>fp16 per 32 K, vfmacc.vf on 64 lanes</td><td>fp16 per 32 K, vfmacc.vf on 64 lanes</td></tr>
<tr><td>inner instruction</td><td>vmerge + vwredsum</td><td>vsub.vx + vadd.vx (masked)</td><td>nds.vd4dots.vv</td></tr>
<tr><td>K reduction</td><td>horizontal, 32 → 1, per row per 32 K</td><td>none: vertical over time</td><td>4 terms inside the dot, then vertical</td></tr>
<tr><td>per 64 rows × 32 K</td><td class="n">{OPS_PER_SUBTILE['upstream']} vector instr.</td><td class="n">{OPS_PER_SUBTILE['rvv']} vector instr.</td><td class="n">{OPS_PER_SUBTILE['vd4']} vector instr.</td></tr>
<tr><td>needs</td><td>VLEN ≥ 256</td><td>VLEN ≥ 512, K % 128 = 0, rows % 64 = 0</td><td>VLEN ≥ 1024, XAndesVDot, same shape gate</td></tr>
</table></div>
<p>Both repacks keep the exact Q1_0 values and the exact 1152 bytes per tile. They differ only in which of the 8192 sign bits sits at which bit position, so a buffer written for one cannot be read by the other.</p>
</section>
""")

    parts.append(f"""<section id="format">
<h2>The data both sides share</h2>
<p>A Q1_0 weight is one sign bit; the value is <code>+d</code> or <code>−d</code> with one fp16 <code>d</code> per 128 weights. Activations are Q8_0: one int8 code and one fp16 scale per 32 values. One weight block therefore lines up with four activation blocks.</p>
{figure(fig_formats(), "Drawn at 6 px per byte. The teal cells are fp16 scales. The four dashed lines show which 4-byte piece of the sign bits multiplies which Q8_0 block.")}
<p>Every kernel on this page computes the same sum: an integer dot inside each 32-K group, scaled by the activation scale of that group, then by the weight scale of the row. What differs is how many rows and how many K one instruction advances.</p>
{more("Block structs as declared in the source (block_q1_0, block_q8_0, block_q1_0x64 and the sign-bit index)",
      pre(src_q1) + pre(src_q8) + pre(src_x64))}
</section>
""")

    parts.append(f"""<section id="weights">
<h2>Weight memory: 1152 bytes, three orders</h2>
<p>Upstream stores 64 independent records of 18 bytes. Both repacks gather the 64 records of one 128-K block into one <code>block_q1_0x64</code>: all 64 scales first, then 1024 bytes of sign bits in the order the reader wants.</p>
{figure(fig_weight_strips(), "Same 1152 bytes, 0.75 px per byte. The outlined box is what one mask load takes: 4, 8 or 32 bytes. Upstream also spreads the 64 scales through the tile, one every 18 bytes; the repacks make them one 128-byte vector load.")}
<p>The repack is done once, when the CPU backend builds its weight buffer. It is a pure permutation of bits: for every sign bit at (row j, column c) it computes a destination bit index and ORs the bit in. The two orders come from one function, so the writer and every reader agree by construction.</p>
{more("Bit-index formulas with the repack writer that applies them (repack.h, repack.cpp)",
      "<p>Default order: <code>c·64 + j</code>, so column c is one 64-bit mask. VD4DOT order: <code>(c/4)·256 + 4j + c%4</code>, so a 256-bit plane holds four columns and mask bit <code>4j + r</code> becomes byte lane <code>4j + r</code> after expansion, which is exactly the operand shape of the dot.</p>" + pre(src_writer))}
</section>
""")

    parts.append(f"""<section id="upstream">
<h2>Layout 1 · Upstream: one row at a time</h2>
<p>The model file stores Q1_0 row by row, so the upstream dot product works on one output row. For each 32-K group it loads 32 sign bits as a mask, loads the 32 activation codes as a vector, selects <code>+a</code> or <code>−a</code> per lane, and then reduces the 32 lanes to one number. At VLEN = 1024 a register holds 128 int8 lanes, so 96 of them idle in every step.</p>
{figure(fig_upstream_flow(), "Upstream data flow for one row and one 32-K group. Lane colour: purple = activation lanes in use, grey = idle. The funnel is the horizontal reduction that ends every group.")}
{pre(UPSTREAM_INNER)}
<p>Cost drivers: the 32-lane vector width is fixed by the 4-byte mask, the horizontal reduction runs once per row per 32 K, and both scales are applied with scalar float multiplies. Nothing here is shared across rows.</p>
{more("Full upstream kernel source (ggml_vec_dot_q1_0_q8_0_vl256, arch/riscv/quants.c)", pre(src_up))}
</section>
""")

    parts.append(f"""<section id="rvv">
<h2>Layout 2 · RVV repack: one column across 64 rows</h2>
<p>The repack turns the work axis by 90 degrees. One 8-byte mask load now brings the sign of column c for all 64 rows. The activation code <code>a[c]</code> is one scalar byte, broadcast by the <code>.vx</code> form of add and subtract. Each of the 64 lanes is one output row's accumulator, so the K sum grows vertically over the loop and the horizontal reduction disappears.</p>
{figure(fig_rvv_flow(), "RVV repack data flow for one column of one 32-K group. Mask bit j and accumulator lane j line up, so the masked add applies the sign per row. Blue = sign bit 1, light blue = sign bit 0 (sample bits).")}
{pre(RVV_INNER)}
<p>The subtract-then-masked-add pair computes <code>±a[c]</code> without materialising a signed vector: all lanes take <code>−a</code>, then lanes whose sign bit is 1 add <code>2a</code>. The weight scales are one <code>vle16.v</code> plus an integer fp16-to-f32 expand, applied once per 128 K with a vector FMA.</p>
{more("Full RVV repack gemv and gemm kernels at VLEN = 1024 (q1_gemv_64x1_vl1024, q1_gemm_64x1_vl1024)",
      pre(src_rvv) + pre(src_rvv_gemm) + "<p>The fp16 scale expand used by every repacked kernel:</p>" + pre(src_expand))}
</section>
""")

    parts.append(f"""<section id="vd4">
<h2>Layout 3 · VD4DOT repack: four columns in every lane</h2>
<p><code>nds.vd4dots.vv</code> multiplies four adjacent int8 pairs and adds the four products into one int32 lane. So the repack groups four columns first: a 32-byte plane holds columns 4q..4q+3 of all 64 rows, with bits 4j..4j+3 belonging to row j. After one mask load and one merge, the register is 256 signed bytes = 64 rows × 4 columns. The four activation codes are read as one 32-bit word and broadcast into every lane. One instruction then advances all 64 rows by four columns.</p>
{figure(fig_vd4_flow(), "VD4DOT data flow for one 4-column quad. The dotted lines show lane 0 and lane 63: bytes 4j..4j+3 of w and s meet in int32 lane j. Orange = sign +1, light orange = sign −1 (sample bits); purple tints = the four activation bytes of the quad.")}
{pre(VD4_INNER, "asm")}
<p>Two shape rules keep the instruction fed. The activation quad is broadcast with <code>vmv.v.x</code> from a general register, so the 32-bit operand comes from an aligned scalar load. All e32 work sits in one asm block, so one <code>vsetvli</code> covers four dots and their four broadcasts, and the e8 mask work is grouped ahead of it.</p>
{more("Full VD4DOT gemv kernel and both asm helpers (q1_gemv_64_vd4dot_vl1024, q1_vd4dots_x4_m2, q1_vd4dots_4acc_m2)",
      pre(src_vd4_asm) + pre(src_vd4_asm4) + pre(src_vd4))}
</section>
""")

    parts.append(f"""<section id="activations">
<h2>Activation memory: where the codes and scales come from</h2>
<p>The activation row is quantized once per matmul. For a single row (gemv, decode) it is a stream of 34-byte <code>block_q8_0</code>. For four rows at once (gemm, prefill) it is a 136-byte <code>block_q8_0x4</code> that interleaves the four rows byte by byte. Upstream and the RVV repack read these as they are. The VD4DOT kernels need 4-byte aligned quads of one row, so each prepares the codes once per call.</p>
{figure(fig_act_gemv(), "gemv: the Q8_0 stream at 6 px per byte, with the 4-byte address grid on top. The scales (teal) push the codes to byte 2 of each record. Below: the aligned copy the VD4DOT gemv reads its quads from.")}
<p>The copy costs one byte-vector load and store per 32-K group and is reused by every 64-row tile of the call. The activation scales are not copied: they are read as scalars from the stream when the group's sum is scaled.</p>
{figure(fig_act_gemm(), "gemm: block_q8_0x4 stores column c of all four rows side by side. The VD4DOT gemm peels the rows apart once with narrowing shifts (vnsrl), after which each row's codes are contiguous and every quad is aligned. The standard RVV gemm reads the interleaved bytes as scalars directly.")}
<p>In the gemm the de-interleaved rows pay off twice: the four rows share every weight vector, so the 1152-byte weight tile is read once for four output rows, and each of the four dots takes its own quad from its own row.</p>
{more("Activation quantizer for the x4 block and the VD4DOT gemm kernel with its de-interleave (ggml_quantize_mat_q8_0_4x1_generic, q1_gemm_64_vd4dot_vl1024)",

</section>
""")

<h2>Where the two scales are applied</h2>
<p>The integer sums are exact; the scales enter as float multiplies at group and block edges. The repacks move both multiplies from scalar code onto 64 lanes and read the 64 weight scales with one vector load.</p>
<div class="tw"><table>
<tr><th></th><th>weight scale d_w (fp16 per 128 K per row)</th><th>activation scale d_a (fp16 per 32 K)</th></tr>
<tr><td><span class="chip up">Upstream</span></td><td>inside each 18-B record; scalar convert; <code>sumf += d_w · acc</code> once per 128 K per row</td><td>at byte 0 of each 34-B block; <code>acc += d_a · sum</code>, scalar, once per 32 K per row</td></tr>
<tr><td><span class="chip rvv">RVV repack</span></td><td><code>d[64]</code> at the block front; <code>vle16.v</code> + integer expand to 64 × f32 once per block; <code>vfmacc.vv sumf, dx, facc</code></td><td>scalar fp16 → f32; <code>vfmacc.vf facc, d_a, vfcvt(sumi)</code> on 64 lanes once per 32 K</td></tr>
<tr><td><span class="chip vd4">VD4DOT gemv</span></td><td>same as RVV repack</td><td>same as RVV repack, on the int32 dot accumulator</td></tr>
<tr><td><span class="chip vd4">VD4DOT gemm</span></td><td colspan="2">the two scales are folded: <code>vfmul.vf dx, d_a[m]</code> then <code>vfmacc.vv sumf_m, (dx·d_a[m]), vfcvt(acc_m)</code> once per group. Four rows need 4 sumf + 4 acc + dx + w + s + vneg1 = 24 of 32 registers, so there is no room for a per-row facc; the fold gives the same sum with one extra vfmul.</td></tr>
</table></div>
</section>
""")

    parts.append(f"""<section id="measured">
<h2>Measured on the 27B model</h2>
<p>Cycle counts on the Andes hybrid simulator, layer 7, geometric mean over the five nodes that have every stage on both paths. The RVV repack step includes the weight-stream prefetch that ships with it.</p>
<div class="tw"><table>
<tr><th>step</th><th class="n">gemv, decode</th><th class="n">gemm, prefill</th></tr>
<tr><td>upstream → RVV repack</td><td class="n">2.24×</td><td class="n">7.04×</td></tr>
<tr><td>RVV repack → + prefetch</td><td class="n">1.60×</td><td class="n">1.07×</td></tr>
<tr><td>+ prefetch → VD4DOT repack</td><td class="n">3.54×</td><td class="n">2.75×</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>total</b></td><td class="n"><b>12.64×</b></td><td class="n"><b>20.67×</b></td></tr>
</table></div>
<p>Decode is instruction-issue bound, so its gain follows the instruction count in the hero figure. Prefill gains most from the layout itself, because the gemm shares every weight vector across four activation rows.</p>
</section>
""")

    parts.append(f"""<section id="appendix">
<h2>Appendix</h2>
{more("Dispatch: which kernel runs at which VLEN and build flag (ggml_gemv_q1_0_64x1_q8_0)",
      "<p>The repack path is chosen for Q1_0 tensors with K divisible by 128 and rows divisible by 64. The RVV repack has 64-row kernels from VLEN = 512 (i16 m2 / f32 m4) and VLEN = 1024 (i16 m1 / f32 m2). The VD4DOT kernels exist at VLEN = 1024 and are built with <code>GGML_RV_XANDESVDOT=ON</code>, which also switches the sign-bit order.</p>" + pre(src_dispatch))}
{more("Source pointers for every excerpt on this page",
      "<ul>"
      "<li><code>ggml/src/ggml-common.h</code>: block_q1_0, block_q8_0</li>"
      "<li><code>ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.h</code>: block_q1_0x64, q1_0x64_sign_bit, block_q8_0x4</li>"
      "<li><code>ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.cpp</code>: repack_q1_0_to_q1_0_64_bl, ggml_quantize_mat_q8_0_4x1_generic</li>"
      "<li><code>ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c</code>: ggml_vec_dot_q1_0_q8_0_vl256</li>"
      "<li><code>ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/repack.cpp</code>: q1_gemv_64x1_vl1024, q1_gemm_64x1_vl1024, q1_vd4dots_x4_m2, q1_vd4dots_4acc_m2, q1_gemv_64_vd4dot_vl1024, q1_gemm_64_vd4dot_vl1024, q1_expand_fp16_64_m2</li>"
      "<li>measurements: <code>profiling_gemv_27b.md</code>, <code>profiling_gemm_27b.md</code></li>"
      "</ul>")}
{more("How the figures were drawn and checked",
      "<p>Every width is a byte, bit or lane count times one fixed scale per figure: 0.75 px per byte in the weight strips, 6 px per byte in the format and activation strips, 2.25 px per sign bit in the hero tiles, 2 px per i8 lane in the VD4DOT flow. A test suite reads the SVG back and checks each drawn width against the number printed next to it, and that no section shows more than seven blocks before its details.</p>")}
</section>
</main>
""")
    return "".join(parts)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    OUT.write_text(build_html())
    print(OUT, OUT.stat().st_size, "bytes")
